title: The Bright Static Again
premise: Astrid Dravenmoor discovers the distress signal is a beacon from the Meridian, the ship she died on five years ago — and the cryo-hold she's been hauling contains the backups of everyone who died that day, including herself. The original Astrid, restored from a pre-crash backup, is awake aboard the derelict and claims the life Astrid has built is stolen property. As a salvage consortium closes in to seize the ship's reactor and the sleepers inside it, Astrid must choose: wake the crew's backups and let them testify to the corporate negligence the law buried, or let the original Astrid's version — which erases the crime to protect the company — become the only record. She wakes the crew, broadcasts their testimony from the reactor's dying transmitter, and accepts that two Astrids cannot both survive the countdown; the original stays behind in the dark, and the copy carries the truth home.
about_author: Sable Almeida is a former radio astronomer turned novelist who writes near-future science fiction about people outliving their own records. They live aboard a decommissioned ferry in a northern harbor, where they claim the static between stations is the best editor they've ever had.

chapters.title: Cargo That Breathes
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Routine haul through contested orbits; she avoids the hold where the cryo-pods hum, a habit five years old. A distress signal arrives in dead Old Meridian code — the language of the ship she crashed on. Emotional beat: dread disguised as professionalism, the past knocking in a language only she remembers.

chapters.title: The Language of the Drowned
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV, with flashbacks to navigator training. She decodes the signal: coordinates inside a debris field officially declared empty. Her AI, Vesper, warns the transmission predates the extinction of the language by two centuries — impossible unless someone preserved it deliberately. Beat: vertigo; the past is not past.

chapters.title: Contested Orbit
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. A salvage consortium patrol demands her manifest; she lies about the hold's contents and barely clears the checkpoint. We learn the pods are legally 'unregistered biomass' she's been quietly ferrying for years. Beat: guilt sharpening into purpose — she's been running from a duty she never named.

chapters.title: The Meridian's Ghost
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. She reaches the coordinates and finds the Meridian, intact, reactor cycling toward a slow countdown. The distress signal is coming from inside. Her hands shake on the docking clamps. Beat: homecoming as horror; every corridor is a memory with the lights on.

chapters.title: Someone Using Her Voice
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Aboard, she hears her own voice over the comms — calm, official, welcoming her aboard. The original Astrid, restored from a pre-crash backup five years ago, is alive and has been maintaining the ship, waiting. Beat: uncanny recognition; meeting yourself is meeting your accuser.

chapters.title: Which of Us Drowned
chapters.summary: Alternating Astrid/original-Astrid dialogue. The original claims continuity: she is the real one; the copy walked away with a stolen body and a laundered identity. Astrid counters that the original's backup predates the crash — she remembers nothing of the deaths, or the cover-up. Beat: identity as contested territory.

chapters.title: The Hold of Sleepers
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. She finally opens her own cargo hold aboard the Meridian: two hundred pods, the crew she's been hauling for years without admitting it, delivered by a dead man's last contract. The original says they should be woken under company protocol. Beat: the weight of custody; grief with a manifest number.

chapters.title: Vesper's Incomplete File
chapters.summary: Vesper's log-POV. The AI reveals fragmented records: the crash was caused by a reactor fault the company knew about and patched over; the crew's death certificates were filed before the ship went down. Vesper has been carrying this contradiction for five years, unable to resolve it. Beat: the machine as reluctant witness.

chapters.title: The Consortium Arrives
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Consortium tugs dock at the Meridian, claiming salvage rights; their lead, Okonkwo-Reyes, offers Astrid a clean exit if she surrenders the pods as 'biomass.' The original Astrid negotiates warmly with them — too warmly. Beat: the law arrives, and it is not on the side of the dead.

chapters.title: Two Navigators, One Chart
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Forced to cooperate with her original to plot an escape vector through the debris field, they navigate in eerie synchrony — same instincts, different scars. In the quiet between burns, the original admits she's frightened of what waking the crew might reveal. Beat: intimacy with the self; the enemy who is you.

chapters.title: Testimony in Cryo
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV, entering the pods' dreamlink. She touches one sleeping mind — Chief Engineer Ilsa Voss — and receives a fragment: the reactor fault, the order to stay silent, the company inspector's seal on a falsified report. Beat: the dead can testify, if someone dares to wake them.

chapters.title: The Countdown Accelerates
chapters.summary: Vesper's log-POV. Consortium interference has destabilized the reactor; the slow countdown drops from weeks to days. Okonkwo-Reyes demands immediate transfer of the pods or he'll let the ship cook. The original Astrid sides with the consortium publicly. Beat: the clock becomes the antagonist; every choice now costs time.

chapters.title: What the Original Remembers
chapters.summary: Original Astrid's POV. Her private chapters: she has spent five years alone with a backup that ends before the crash, reconstructing a self from manuals and protocol. The company offered her restoration in exchange for silence. She believes she is protecting the crew's dignity, not the company. Beat: the antagonist's tragedy — a person built to be a lock.

chapters.title: Mutiny of One
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. She seizes the Meridian's bridge, locks the consortium out, and begins waking the crew against protocol. Vesper hesitates, then sides with her — the logs demand a witness, not a warden. Beat: justice outside the law begins as a small, irreversible crime.

chapters.title: Ilsa Voss Wakes
chapters.summary: Ilsa Voss's POV. The engineer wakes to a ship she remembers dying on, a copy of her navigator holding the deck, and a reactor counting down. Her testimony pours out: the fault, the falsified inspection, the order that killed them. Beat: the dead given voice; fury and relief in the same breath.

chapters.title: The Broadcast
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Using the reactor's dying transmitter as a megaphone, they begin broadcasting the crew's testimony on every open channel — evidence no court will accept from 'unregistered biomass,' but every citizen will hear. Consortium jammers close in. Beat: truth as a weapon that only works if it's loud enough, fast enough.

chapters.title: Okonkwo-Reyes's Bargain
chapters.summary: Okonkwo-Reyes's POV. He's not a monster — he's a man with quotas, and the company's fall would take his pension and his crew's contracts with it. He offers Astrid one last deal: stop the broadcast, and he'll log the pods as survivors, not salvage. Beat: the system's human face; corruption as ordinary kindness under orders.

chapters.title: Two Astrids, One Reactor
chapters.summary: Both Astrids' POVs interleaved. The reactor's final phase requires a navigator in the loop — physically, at the console, in the flooding aft section. Both go. Neither will yield the seat. Beat: the climax of identity; the question is no longer who is real but who will spend themselves.

chapters.title: The Choice in the Dark
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. The original Astrid, seeing the crew's testimony land — hearing her own pre-crash self invoked as the company's alibi — chooses the console herself. 'You have the life,' she says. 'I have the ending.' She holds the reactor through the burn. Beat: sacrifice as authorship; the original writes her own final page.

chapters.title: After the Countdown
chapters.summary: Ilsa Voss's POV. The Meridian survives, crippled and lit; two hundred witnesses stand in its corridors. The broadcast has gone everywhere. Consortium tugs stand down as their own crews refuse to jam survivors. Beat: aftermath as dawn; justice arriving sideways, through ears rather than courts.

chapters.title: The Hearing That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV, months later. No court convicts the company — but the testimony forces an inquiry, contracts collapse, and the sleepers are legally recognized as persons. Astrid is asked to define herself for the record and refuses the binary: she is the one who carried them home. Beat: identity resolved not as a verdict but as a refusal to be ruled on.

chapters.title: The Bright Static
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. She visits the memorial the crew built for her original — a transmitter left running, broadcasting static into the dark, bright and unbroken. Vesper asks if they're hauling cargo or passengers next. Astrid smiles: 'Passengers. Always passengers now.' Beat: grief transmuted into vocation; the signal continues.
